facts.claim: "Welcome to Hard Times" is the opening and title track of Charley Crockett's eighth album, released July 31, 2020 on Son of Davy.
The song is credited to Charley Crockett as sole writer, and its length is listed as 3:08.
The album was produced by Mark Neill, and it includes songwriting contributions from Dan Auerbach and Pat McLaughlin.
Crockett says he wrote most of the record, including the title track, in November 2019 and recorded the whole thing in February 2020. He finished about a month before the pandemic upended America.
Crockett recalled that the album was cut at Mark Neill's studio, where a yellow rotary phone sat on the desk.
Discogs lists the album as produced at Soil Of The South Studios.
Crockett has said that when he wrote the title song he was writing about what he was seeing, not about the pandemic.
The title track was the first single from the album. Crockett said it drew the strongest response of any of his singles so far, including from people who had given up on country music.
Crockett has described Welcome to Hard Times as a hardcore gothic country record and tied it to his 'Gulf and Western' sound.
The album came after Crockett's open-heart surgery. He says he wanted to make an album that would change the entire conversation about country music.

research.lineage: The song sits in a retro, 1960s-style country-western tradition that Crockett calls 'Gulf and Western', which blends country with New Orleans soul and R&B, blues and Texas troubadour roots.

draft:
**Welcome to Hard Times** opens with a pitch. Crockett plays the barker at the door of a rigged house, telling everyone (boys and girls, women, children, you and him) that life is a casino and the dice are loaded. Even a hobo, he adds, could tell you that much. It's a dry joke, and the chorus leans into it with the cheerful menace of a host who knows how your night will end: "Do you like sinnin'? No? / Well, you will before you go." The welcome is warm. The room is crooked. That gap is where the song lives.

The band plays it the way that host would want, relaxed and unbothered. An acoustic guitar keeps a steady rhythm, a walking bass strolls underneath, and the drums hold a simple beat with brushes. The swing is slight, the tempo easy. A clean electric guitar works a melodic line around the vocal, and nobody harmonizes with Crockett. The voice stands alone, clear with a little rasp, delivered like conversation across a bar. The room sounds dry and close. Nothing here pleads for attention, which makes the bad news land harder.

This is the sound Crockett calls Gulf and Western: 1960s country-western blended with New Orleans soul and R&B, blues, and Texas troubadour roots. He has called the album a hardcore gothic country record. The title track bends the dance-hall shuffle toward something darker. The groove invites you to two-step while the words describe a fixed game.

Then the second verse drops the act. Crockett asks you to look in his eyes and see past the bright lights spread in front of him, and the barker turns into someone wondering whether anyone would notice him at all: "If I told you my life just isn't fair?" The question is half self-pity and half a dare, and the song won't say which. It doesn't wait for an answer. The chorus comes right back, mask on, still selling sin and lies. The pride and the hurt sit side by side and never settle. The final line pushes the welcome one step further, into a hope that you're feeling it too.

Crockett wrote it in November 2019, after open-heart surgery, and cut the record in February 2020 at producer Mark Neill's studio, a month before the pandemic upended the country. He has said he was writing about what he saw, not about what came next. It was the album's first single and drew the strongest response of any he'd released, including from people who had given up on country music.

The song gets you smiling along with the man running the crooked table, and then it makes you wonder who is going to look him in the eye.
